---
title: "How name matching works"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(geopt)
```

`pt_match()` looks simple from the outside. This article explains the steps
behind it, and *why* they are the way they are: the design follows from
measured facts about Portuguese place names.

## The problem, quantified

Matching names to units would be trivial if names were unique. They are
not:

```{r stats}
codes <- pt_lookup()
tf <- table(codes$freguesia)
sum(tf > 1)                    # freguesia names used by more than one freguesia
head(sort(tf, decreasing = TRUE), 3)

mun <- unique(codes[, c("municipio", "distrito_ilha")])
mun$municipio[duplicated(mun$municipio)]   # ambiguous municipality names
```

At municipality level, only one name is shared: Lagoa, in Faro district and
on São Miguel. At freguesia level, shared names are the norm: about 200 names
are used more than once, some six times. But no municipality has two
freguesias with the same name, so knowing the municipality always settles it.
That fact shapes the whole design: *narrowing the search with a context is
the core of the matcher, not an extra*.

## The steps

For each input, in order:

1. **Codes.** Strings of digits have any lost leading zeros restored and are
   checked against the level's codes; strings like `"PT11A"` are accepted at
   NUTS levels. Codes never go through name matching.
2. **The name as given.** Tried first, exactly, before anything is taken
   apart. This matters because over a hundred current freguesia names, and
   265 pre-2013 ones, *end* in brackets (`"Bouro (Santa Maria)"`,
   `"Ílhavo (São Salvador)"`), and a real name must never be mistaken for a
   name followed by a region.
3. **A region in brackets.** Only if step 2 fails: in `"Lagoa (Açores)"` or
   `"Calheta [R.A.M.]"`, the part in brackets is taken off and used as the
   context. INE's `R.A.A.` and `R.A.M.` forms are understood. A region after a
   dash (`"Calheta - RAA"`) is only split off when it's a recognized region,
   so `"Albergaria-a-Velha"` stays in one piece.
4. **Cleaning** (`pt_normalize()`): lowercase, expand `S.`, `Sta.` and `Sto.`,
   remove accents and punctuation. Cleaning makes almost no names collide
   that didn't already (196 shared freguesia names become 199), which is why
   it's safe to apply to everything.
5. **Aliases**, cleaned the same way. They're checked before any name is
   matched: the way to handle a source's own spellings.
6. **Exact match, within the context.** If there's a context (from the
   argument or from brackets), only the units inside it are considered.
7. **Name and context combined.** With a context, `"Sé"` + `"Braga"` is also
   tried as `"Sé (Braga)"` and `"Braga (Sé)"`; see *Two ways to spell the same
   freguesia* below.
8. **Ignoring small words.** `"ULS da Guarda"` matches `"ULS Guarda"`, and
   `"Senhora da Graça de Padrões"` matches `"…dos Padrões"`. An exact spelling
   always wins; this step only runs when nothing matched exactly. The report
   marks these matches as `"loose"`.
9. **Fuzzy matching**, if requested, on whatever is still unmatched.

Step 6 also checks a short internal list of known variants: spellings INE uses
that aren't the official name (`"Passos"` and `"Paços"`), a ULS's name before
2024, and units whose official name has a qualifier added to tell it apart, so
the plain name doesn't appear anywhere (`"Calheta"` for
`"Calheta de São Jorge"`).

## Two vintages of names

In 2013, about half of all freguesias were merged into uniões, so a name read
off an older census file often has no current counterpart. `pt_match()`
matches those too (`historic = TRUE`, the default), and returns the unit that
covers that territory today:

```{r historic}
pt_match(c("Sé", "Maximinos", "Cividade"), level = "freguesia",
         context = "Braga", quiet = TRUE)
```

All three were merged into one união in 2013. The report labels them, which
tells a match on an old name apart from a match on a current one:

```{r historic-report}
pt_match_report(pt_match(c("Sé", "Gualtar"), level = "freguesia",
                         context = "Braga", quiet = TRUE))
```

The code returned is the current one. `admin_vintage` asks for another
vintage's code instead. Because each name matched a *particular* old
freguesia, it can return that one, rather than only the união that covers all
three:

```{r historic-to}
pt_match(c("Sé", "Maximinos", "Cividade"), level = "freguesia",
         context = "Braga", admin_vintage = "2011", quiet = TRUE)
```

This works by matching against that vintage's names directly, not by looking
up a column: a current freguesia can have up to 12 pre-2013 predecessors,
which don't fit in a table with one row per current freguesia. A *current*
name doesn't point to any one predecessor, so with `admin_vintage = "2011"` it
only matches when the freguesia had exactly one. Otherwise it returns `NA`,
since nothing says which of them was meant.

This is the one place where a name can mean two different units, so the
order matters: **a name still in use always wins over an old one.** 161
pre-2013 names are spelled the same as a current freguesia that is a
different unit. Figueira da Foz's `"Alhadas"`, for example, is both a current
freguesia and the name of a 2013 união that was later split up. If old and
current names were treated as equals, all of those would become ambiguous,
and 166 bare names that resolve to a current freguesia would return `NA`
instead. So when both an old and a current name match, only the current one is
kept.

It follows that historic matching never changes how a current name resolves:
every current freguesia matches the same way with `historic = TRUE` and
`historic = FALSE`.

When an old freguesia's territory was later split between several current
ones, its name really is ambiguous, and is reported that way: pass a context
or use codes. Old names are matched exactly, or ignoring small words, but
never fuzzily. An old name already involves a guess about which vintage was
meant, and letting a typo make a second guess would produce a match nobody
could check.

## Two ways to spell the same freguesia

INE prefixes a city's pre-2013 freguesias with the city — `"Braga (Sé)"`,
`"Beja (Salvador)"` — but names the same kind of unit plainly elsewhere
(`"Sé"` in Lisboa, Porto and Portalegre). All the spellings resolve:

```{r spellings}
pt_match(c("Braga (Sé)", "Sé (Braga)"), level = "freguesia", quiet = TRUE)
```

The names are stored exactly as INE publishes them. The other spellings are
built from the name and the context at match time (step 7), rather than
listed in advance. A bare `"Sé"` with no context stays ambiguous: six cities
had one.

## Deliberately strict

Three behaviours are strict on purpose:

* **An ambiguous name gives `NA` and a warning, never a guess.** A wrong
  Lagoa that nobody notices ends up as a wrong published map.
* **An unrecognized context gives `NA`.** If a misspelled
  `context = "Nrte"` were quietly ignored, an ambiguous name would be matched
  without it, which is exactly the wrong-namesake mistake a context exists to
  prevent.
* **Fuzzy matching is off unless requested, and cautious when on.** It only
  runs on names that didn't match exactly, only accepts a candidate that is
  clearly closer than the next best, never picks between units that share a
  name, and reports every match it makes. The context matters most here: it
  cuts the candidates from about 3,000 names to a few dozen, which is what
  makes matching by spelling distance safe at all.

Every decision is recorded in the report attached to the result:

```{r report}
res <- pt_match(c("0115", "Lagoa (Faro)", "Lagoa", "Atlantis"), quiet = TRUE)
pt_match_report(res)
```

## Why the echarts renderer keys by code

The same shared names explain a detail of `plot_pt()`. An echarts map links
data to shapes **by name**. If the shapes were registered under their names,
the two Lagoas couldn't be told apart, and one would quietly get the other's
value. So the echarts renderer registers each shape under its official code,
and only turns codes back into names for the tooltips.

## Where the names come from

The official names and codes are CAOP's, through `pt_registry` (one row per
freguesia; see *How the bundled data is built*). Matching at a level uses that
level's name columns. For freguesias, that's both the official name and CAOP's
simplified name (`designacao_simplificada`), so either spelling matches.

The 2013 freguesias have the last name each carried on that map, as in CAOP
2024 (DGT's last release of it) and in INE's tables, which agree on every one.
25 of them were renamed by law while the map was in force, and DGT corrected a
few spellings. Those earlier names are names of the 2013 map too, so they
match there even with `historic = FALSE`:

```{r names-2013}
pt_match(c("Buarcos", "Buarcos e São Julião"), level = "freguesia",
         context = "Figueira da Foz", admin_vintage = "2013",
         historic = FALSE, quiet = TRUE)
```

Pre-2013 names are the `"2011"` and `"2001"` vintages of `pt_registry`. They
come from INE's code lists for those two censuses: indicator 0006393 for 2011,
whose 4,260 codes are exactly the map in force before 2013, and indicator
0000535 for 2001, with 4,241 (see `data-raw/fetch_2011_names.R` and
`data-raw/fetch_2001_registry.R`).

Most 2001 names are also 2011 names, and a few of those freguesias lost
territory in between: São Salvador, in Odemira, gave part of its land to two
new freguesias in 2001. So a 2001 name is only used when no later vintage has
it. `"Odemira (São Salvador)"` keeps its 2011 meaning, which is one freguesia
today, while `"Agualva-Cacém"`, which was split in 2001, is matched from the
2001 map.
